To the Editor-in-Chief, Applied Energy

Dear Editor,

Please consider the manuscript "%%TITLE%%" as a Full Length Research Article.

After a demand-response event, utilities and aggregators must restore deferred charging energy to electric vehicles before their owners leave. One feeder limit caps the total. Some vehicles silently fail to resume charging. Vehicle clouds can confirm delivery 30 to 60 minutes late. The paper asks what an operator gains from planning, from one shared model of silent failure and from reliability learned per participant.

What the paper shows:

- A two-slot example bounds the loss of a scheduler that cannot tell unreliable participants apart. It also bounds the share that earlier events recover.
- On a synthetic benchmark with a frozen protocol, at a 30-minute delay and a loose feeder limit, a planner with one shared failure rate captured {{confirm/C3}} of the gain of a planner that learns per-participant reliability. Under a tight limit the share fell from a 15-minute to a 60-minute delay.
- Five frozen tests held on 200 held-out random instances, with 99% intervals adjusted for five tests. Two of the five were found post hoc in development.
- Learning who fails was worth more at delays of 30 to 60 minutes than at 0 to 15 minutes. It helped inside the planner and not inside the two greedy rules tested.
- A dedicated section states what a utility pilot must log and measure to confirm or refute the main share.

Fit to the journal's scope. The work addresses applied energy problems the journal lists: demand response, flexibility, smart grid operation and optimization methods for energy systems. It links a scheduling result to the data a utility pilot would need, which bridges research and implementation.

The manuscript is not published and is not under review elsewhere. Preprint status: TO CONFIRM BY THE AUTHOR (arXiv posting planned or not yet posted). All data are synthetic.
